title: A cauldron of unholy loves (3.1)
tomorrow: what book could set a bored student's heart on fire?

lines: FIRST NIGHT IN A NEW CITY.
cards: First night in a new city. Music through the wall, ads on every bus, a party somewhere down the hall, and everyone around you chasing something. Augustine knew that night.
Book three of the Confessions opens with him arriving to study, far from his mother's house. In Pusey's translation: "To Carthage I came." Four plain words.
And what was singing in his ears? He tells us. All around him, he says, sang "a cauldron of unholy loves."

teach.b: His Latin word for the cauldron is sartago, a frying pan, and the city is Carthago; some readers hear the city itself sizzling. Notice what's in the pan: loves. Not hatred.
Augustine's trouble in Carthage is that he loves badly, too fast, in the wrong directions. Then a line that cuts close.
He wasn't in love yet, he says, but he loved to love.
He was starving for an inner food, God himself, and didn't feel the hunger.
So he went looking for something to love, and found it came with jealousy, suspicion, fear, anger and quarrels, like being beaten with burning iron rods, in his words. A cauldron isn't only a place.
It's an atmosphere: what everyone around you is loving, chasing, watching and wanting, all bubbling at once. What Augustine gives a person this week is a way to stand in it.

teach.h: NAME THE HEAT, NOT BLAME IT.
teach.b: He doesn't blame the city for his choices. He names the heat honestly, and he names his own hunger underneath it.
The restless heart from his first page is the same heart in Carthage, still hungry, looking in the wrong pans.

how: In Catholic spiritual direction, a director may ask not only about a person's choices but about the surroundings and habits that shape what they love.

games.q: what does “a cauldron of unholy loves” mean?
o: a witch's pot in an old African legend
a city that hated anyone who believed in God
a city bubbling with loves aimed the wrong way

p: Latin: a frying pan, a cauldron
in love with being in love

s: Augustine blames Carthage for everything he did there
he names the heat honestly, but he owns his choices.
the cauldron is full of hatred
it's full of loves, aimed the wrong way.
he says he loved to love before he was in love
he was hungry for an inner food, God, and didn't feel it.

games.q: your cousin starts at a big office where everyone flexes weekend spending, and he's started to as well. what does Augustine's cauldron give him?
o: name the heat, and notice which of his loves it pulls on.
quit; a place like that will ruin anyone no matter what.
join in fully; to fit in you have to love what they love.
games.why: Augustine neither blames the city nor pretends the heat isn't there. he names it, and the hunger underneath.

practice: Make a small plan, in three quiet steps. Name the cauldron you live in: the feed, the mood at work or school, whatever the people around you are chasing. Name the one pull it has on your loves.
Then choose one small thing you'll do the next time that heat rises, and hold that plan in mind until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: A cauldron of unholy loves. Augustine's picture of Carthage: a city bubbling with loves aimed the wrong way, and a young man who loved to love.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 3.1: a frying pan or cauldron; some readers hear a play on Carthago.

carryVoice: The line to keep: carthage, the heat he named instead of blaming. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Augustine, Confessions 3.1.1 (loved to love; inner famine; iron rods)
